name: Incident notice
description: Sent while something is broken: the severity, what is affected, what is not, and the time the next update will arrive.

origin.note: Design: incident — severity first, the blast radius as a matched pair of columns, and the next-update time set as the specimen of the page.

subject: {{ severity_label }} — {{ impact_headline }}
preheader: What is affected, what is not, and the time the next update lands.

severity_level.description: Drives the banner's weight, glyph and colour. Use `danger` for an outage, `warning` for degraded service. Severity is carried by the word as well as the colour, so it survives a client that repaints it.

severity_label.description: Your own severity vocabulary, so the reader can match this against your status page and your contract. Leads the subject line.

impact_line.description: The banner sentence: what a customer cannot do right now. Written from their side of the API, not ours.
impact_line.example: Messages sent through the EU region are failing.

impact_headline.description: The headline, and the rest of the subject line. Name the symptom, not the suspected cause — the cause changes during an incident and the symptom does not.
impact_headline.example: Sending is failing in the EU region

started_at.description: When impact began, not when you noticed. The gap between the two is the number a customer will reconstruct anyway, so state it yourself.

timezone.description: The timezone both times on this page are given in, with its offset. An incident email is read in every timezone you sell into, so this is never implicit.

summary.description: What is known, in two or three sentences. No hedging and no 'some users may have experienced' — say what is failing and what you are doing. If the cause is unknown, say that it is unknown.
summary.example: Requests to the EU sending endpoint are returning 500s. We have confirmed the failure is in the EU region only and are rolling back a change released at 13:30.

affected_text.description: What is broken, in one short paragraph. Specific enough that a reader can tell whether it touches them.
affected_text.example: The EU sending endpoint, and any send scheduled to leave from it since 13:42.

unaffected_text.description: What is still working. Naming this is what stops a regional fault being read as a total outage, and it is the half of the email most senders leave out.
unaffected_text.example: The US region, the dashboard, webhooks, and everything already delivered. No data has been lost.

next_update_at.description: The clock time of the next update — the single most important line in this email. A promised time you keep is what makes the next incident email get opened.

next_update_note.description: The cadence under the time, so the reader knows whether to sit and watch or to go away and come back.
next_update_note.default: and every 30 minutes after that, whether or not anything has changed.

status_url.description: The live status page, which is where a reader should go rather than into your support queue.

status_label.description: Label for the status page action.

closing.description: The closing line. Say who is reachable and how — during an incident this line is doing customer support on its own.
closing.default: Replies to this email reach the engineers working on it. You do not need to open a ticket.
